The Problem: Sending Notifications
Imagine you're building a notification system for an app. It needs to send alerts to users through different delivery channels:
["Email: for formal, detailed messaging","SMS: for short, instant alerts"]

blocks.content: The first instinct might be to just subclass everything:
Here is what this class hierarchy looks like:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245783376-2841787b.png
Every node here is doing two jobs at once it knows what kind of notification it is AND how to deliver it. That's already a red flag, and we only have 2 types with 2 channels.
Where This Design Starts to Hurt
blocks.text: Where This Design Starts to Hurt

blocks.content: 1. Class Explosion
The number of classes grows with every new addition:
["2 types × 2 channels = 4 classes","Introduce PushNotification as a third channel? That's 6 classes","Add WarningNotification or PromoNotification? The count keeps multiplying"]
items: 2 types × 2 channels = 4 classes
Introduce PushNotification as a third channel? That's 6 classes
Add WarningNotification or PromoNotification? The count keeps multiplying

blocks.content: Maintaining this becomes a full-time job.
2. Tight Coupling
The notification logic and the delivery logic are glued together inside every subclass. There's no way to reuse the SMS sending behavior without it being tied to a specific notification type.
3. Violates Open/Closed Principle
Every time a new delivery channel is introduced, you have to go back and create a new subclass for each and every existing notification type. Nothing is truly reusable or extensible.
What a Better Design Looks Like

blocks.content: This is exactly the gap the Bridge Pattern fills.
2. What is the Bridge Pattern?
The Bridge Pattern lets you cut a class into two separate hierarchies one for the abstraction, one for the implementation so both sides can grow without getting in each other's way.
Two core ideas define it:

1. Independent Variation The abstraction side (notification types) and the implementation side (delivery channels) evolve on their own terms. Adding a new notification type doesn't touch any channel logic. Adding a new channel doesn't touch any notification class.

2. Composition over Inheritance Instead of inheriting behavior, the abstraction holds a reference to an implementor and delegates work to it at runtime. This keeps both hierarchies lean and easy to extend.

Think of a smartphone and a wireless speaker. The phone is the abstraction it has controls for play, pause, and volume. The speaker is the implementation it contains the actual hardware that produces sound. You can connect the same phone to a JBL or a Sony speaker without changing anything on the phone. You can control a JBL with an iPhone or an Android without changing anything on the speaker. The two sides vary completely independently, linked only by the Bluetooth connection between them. That connection is the bridge.

blocks.content: The Four Moving Parts

1. Abstraction Notification The front-facing layer your app talks to. It holds a reference to a Sender object and defines notify(msg) in domain terms. It knows what to communicate not how to deliver it.

2. RefinedAbstraction Alert, Reminder Concrete subclasses that bring their own purpose and urgency. Alert handles critical messages, Reminder handles scheduled nudges. Neither one touches delivery logic they just call the Sender and let it do its job.

3. Implementor Sender The interface on the other side of the bridge. It declares the send(msg) contract that every delivery channel must fulfill. This is what keeps the two hierarchies loosely connected without being tangled.

4. ConcreteImplementors Email, SMS The actual workers. Email formats and dispatches an email. SMS fires off a text message. Neither knows whether it was triggered by an Alert or a Reminder that's not their concern.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245784114-26320d5a.png

Step 1: Create a concrete implementor The client instantiates a specific delivery channel for example EmailSender. This object knows exactly how to deliver a message via email. That is the only thing it knows.

Step 2: Pass it to the abstraction The client creates an Alert and injects the EmailSender through its constructor. The Alertstores this reference internally. It does not know or care what kind of sender it received.

Step 3: Call the high-level operation The client calls alert.notify(msg). This is a domain-level operation: "send this notification." The client thinks in terms of notifications, not delivery channels.

Step 4: Abstraction delegates to implementor Inside notify(), the Alert calls sender.send(msg). It translates the high-level intent ("notify someone") into a low-level instruction ("deliver this message") and hands it off to the implementor.
Step 5: Implementor executes The EmailSender runs its own delivery logic and dispatches the email. It has no idea it was triggered by an Alert. It simply received a message and did its job.
4. Implementing the Bridge Pattern
Let's build the notification system step by step, decoupling the notification type from the delivery channel.

This interface declares the delivery contract. Every concrete channel must implement it.
